title: Made in Germany: The Post-War Export Boom
abstract: Chapter 4 of Vonyó's monograph 'The Economic Consequences of the War: West Germany's Growth Miracle after 1945' (Cambridge University Press 2018). Analyses the post-war West German export boom and its role in the country's recovery. No publisher-side chapter abstract available.
summary_en: Why did West Germany's post-1945 export miracle take off? In Chapter 4 of his Cambridge UP monograph on the West German growth miracle, Vonyó argues that the boom was less a direct gift of the Marshall Plan than the cumulative product of pre-war industrial capability, an undervalued Deutschemark after 1949, and the rapid re-integration of West Germany into European trade through the EPU and later the EEC. Recovery of German exports tracked the recovery of European demand, with manufacturing capacity ready to absorb it.
data_used: Historical narrative drawing on West German trade statistics, Marshall Plan and OEEC archival series, the Bundesbank long-run macroeconomic series, and the existing economic-history literature. No econometric estimation in this chapter; quantitative tables drawn from official sources.
policy_relevance: Indirectly relevant for Hungarian export-led-growth strategy (HIPA, ITM industrial policy): the West German episode is the canonical case of recovery driven by a competitive exchange rate plus restored access to trading-bloc demand, both of which Hungary itself drew on after 1990 and again post-2004. The chapter is a useful corrective to Marshall-Plan-centric narratives — it puts integrating into a bigger market and keeping unit labour costs competitive at the centre of the story.
